body_markdown:
AI is dominating the programmatic advertising conversation. According to the


[IAB’s 2026 Outlook Study](https://www.iab.com/insights/2026-outlook/) , two-thirds of media buyers are focused on agentic AI for ad buying and campaign execution. As the industry moves toward more automated media buying, another fundamental consideration deserves renewed attention: privacy.


The shift away from persistent user identifiers has been underway for years. Safari eliminated third-party cookies in 2020, and privacy restrictions continue to expand across browsers, operating systems, and advertising technologies.


These changes have significant implications for programmatic reach. According to


[Statcounter](https://gs.statcounter.com/browser-market-share/mobile/north-america) , Safari represented nearly 46% of North American mobile browser usage in September 2026.


Apple’s latest Safari restrictions reinforce why privacy remains essential to how programmatic advertising is built, targeted, and activated.


## **Apple’s Safari Update: What Changed?**


With iOS 27, Apple introduced additional restrictions targeting identity resolution infrastructure. This technology connects information such as email addresses to persistent identifiers that recognize users across websites.


In an


[October 19 WebKit announcement](https://webkit.org/blog/18438/blocking-identity-resolution-infrastructure/) , Apple confirmed that Safari and WebKit now block network access to certain third-party identity resolution services.


The changes had several notable implications for ad tech:


- **Identity resolution:** Services associated with LiveRamp, ID5, and The Trade Desk’s Unified ID 2.0 were affected, according to


[Digiday](https://digiday.com/marketing/apples-growing-ads-business-puts-its-safari-blocklist-under-scrutiny/) .


- **Ad delivery:** The restrictions also temporarily disrupted The Trade Desk’s ad-serving infrastructure in affected Safari environments.


- **Apple’s response:** Subsequent reporting indicated that Apple restored the ad-serving domain while maintaining restrictions on identity resolution.


The distinction matters. Apple targeted cross-site identity tracking, but the separate ad-serving disruption demonstrated how changes to one component of ad tech can affect another.


For advertisers, the implications are concerning. Continued reliance on persistent user identity leaves audience reach and campaign delivery vulnerable to privacy restrictions and platform changes beyond their control.


## **The Industry Has Moved Beyond Cookies. Has It Moved Beyond Identity?**


The decline of third-party cookies accelerated investment in alternative identifiers, identity graphs, and authenticated audience solutions.


While these technologies serve different purposes, many still depend on recognizing individuals across digital environments. Replacing a cookie with another identifier does not eliminate that dependency.


As Inuvo’s VP of Programmatic Operations and Solutions Engineering, Eric Tilbury, stated:


> “the industry’s overreliance on user identity outside walled gardens creates a fragile foundation. Every new browser policy or privacy restriction can expose another limitation.
>
>
> “


This raises an important question:


**How much of an advertiser’s audience strategy depends on knowing who someone is, rather than understanding what interests them?**


When buying decisions depend heavily on persistent identifiers, advertisers risk overlooking relevant opportunities where those signals are unavailable.


## **The Opportunity: Reaching Audiences Beyond User IDs**


With Safari accounting for nearly half of North American mobile browser usage, advertisers have good reason to examine their reach in environments where persistent identifiers are limited.


Privacy-first programmatic advertising offers opportunities to reach relevant audiences that ID-dependent strategies may overlook. AI-driven approaches that analyze content, context, and emerging intent can inform targeting without relying on individual tracking.


A practical starting point is to test identity-free targeting alongside existing campaigns. Compare incremental reach, delivery across browsers and devices, and performance against business objectives.


These insights can reveal where privacy-first approaches add value and where existing strategies may be leaving opportunities untapped.


## **Applying AI to Privacy-First Programmatic Advertising**


At Inuvo, this approach is foundational to IntentKey, our AI-powered audience intelligence technology.


IntentKey analyzes more than 110 billion URLs across the open web, with over one million additional URLs analyzed daily. Its AI continuously examines billions of signals and their relationships, identifying content consumption patterns that reveal emerging interests, motivations, sentiment, and intent.


These signals are distilled into more than 100 million concept and sentiment data points that dynamically form IntentKey audience models, without identifying or tracking individual consumers.


Models refresh every five minutes, helping advertisers recognize shifts in interest and uncover opportunities beyond traditional identity-based segments. This intelligence can help advertisers anticipate emerging intent up to 24 hours ahead of competing solutions.


IntentKey supports programmatic activation through multiple DSP partners across display, connected TV, online video, and streaming audio. Its identity-free approach removes the need for cookies, mobile advertising IDs, identity graphs, or other personal identifiers for audience targeting.


## **Privacy Must Remain Part of Programmatic Innovation**


As AI transforms programmatic advertising, advertisers must evaluate the intelligence informing their buying decisions alongside the technologies executing them.


Apple’s Safari restrictions reinforce the risks of relying too heavily on persistent user identity. They also highlight an opportunity to expand reach through approaches that understand audience intent without individual tracking.


Advertisers that test privacy-first strategies can uncover opportunities their existing campaigns may be missing and build greater flexibility into their programmatic approach.
